doc.title: Jane Monheit interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, August 20, 2010

title: Using her own band instead of star names in the studio
summary: She argues for her touring band on records, with friends like Mark O'Connor and John Pizzarelli as guests, so records resemble live shows.

story.theme_name: In the studio: making records, then and now
story.community_name: Making records: studios, takes and the technology

blocks.x: Was there a point where — let me rephrase — what had to happen for you to be able to use your band in the studio?

An awful lot. Because I’ve been arguing for them for years. But you know everybody seems to think that it’s going to be a big selling factor if you have a lot of star names on the record. My opinion on that differs. Because I know my audience and I pretty much © Fillius Jazz Archive -6-

believe that with a few exceptions, you know getting a star rhythm section on the album there are going to be names that the people that buy these kind of vocal albums probably won’t recognize, and you’re going to end up with a band of brilliant, brilliant musicians who maybe aren’t that interested in playing with you and you end up getting a record that sounds very nice but isn’t as heartfelt, and you know I tour with my band constantly. I have for years. These guys are my brothers. And they are brilliant musicians. And just because they aren’t stars in their own right necessarily yet, that’s ridiculous to ask me to not play with them on the album. Although, on the other hand, I’ve been lucky to play with a lot of amazing people, and that’s been really cool. But I don’t want to go into the studio without my band, it’s ridiculous. You know I mean why would I want to do that? But then bringing in special guests to add to our core group is the most brilliant thing ever, and it’s amazing, and you’re so lucky to be able to do that in the studio. The cool thing about the new record is all the people we brought in are friends, people I’ve worked with a lot in the past and it was great, and so I wanted to do it again, with the exception of Larry Goldings who plays a tune on the album and is a friend of ours, a friend of the band, but we just hadn’t played together before. But you know Mark O’Connor is on the record, John Pizzarelli is on the record, I mean these are huge names that people will recognize, and people who buy my records will recognize them, because I’ve been on tours with them and recorded with them and done all kinds of stuff with these guys before.
Well those people who go to your concert and buy the thing and want to get it autographed, that’s a plus for them too because they’re going to get what they just heard.

Exactly, that’s the whole point of it. That’s the whole point. That’s what I tell the crowd in the show every night when I’m telling them about the new record. I say it’s been amazing making these great big epic albums with orchestras and the whole thing, and I will do that again because it’s really fun, but it was time to do something that even like remotely resembled what we’re doing every night on stage. You know people come and buy the record after the show, and I’m sending them home with something that is completely different from what they just heard and I feel a little bit weird about that. And then you know we make these records that I can’t play live. So many of the tunes I just don’t even play live. And I’ll tell the producers that in the studio. I’ve done it in the past. You know this song is amazing and this is beautiful, but I’m not going to be able to do this live. Like, “Oh yes you can, oh just try.” “No it’s not going to work, I will never do this live. Most of this record we’re not going to be able to do live, I just want you guys to know that.” And I’ve worked with great producers and I will again but I think in the future I’m going to have to insist on co-producing every project. Because I know what’s right for me. © Fillius Jazz Archive -7-
